lead: Turn the NTFS metadata files of a Windows disk into CSV, JSON or bodyfile output that you can sort and search. MFTECmd is a command-line parser written by Eric Zimmerman.
use_when: You need a list of every file and folder on an NTFS volume, including deleted entries, with all their timestamps.
You want to check whether file times were changed on purpose, by comparing the two sets of timestamps in each record.
You need file system activity from the USN journal ($J) for a timeline.

features.title: Reads NTFS system files
items: The project page also lists $I30 as supported
The project reports that it detects the type of each file from its content
Can read locked files and Volume Shadow Copies through raw disk access

features.title: Output you can use
items: CSV and JSON files written to a folder you choose
Bodyfile output for timeline tools, for the $MFT
Option to set your own output file name

features.title: Looks at one record closely
items: Dumps the full details of one entry by its entry number and sequence number
Can list the contents of a directory entry
Can export a single raw FILE record from a given offset
Can dump the details of one security ID

features.title: Volume Shadow Copies
items: Processes all shadow copies on the drive you point it at
Can remove duplicate files between the live volume and the copies, based on SHA-1

requirements: Windows. The project offers two builds: one for .NET Framework 4.7.2 or newer and one for .NET 10 or newer. You need the matching runtime installed. The project's page also says to unzip with a tool such as 7-Zip and not to run it from Program Files unless you run as administrator.

steps.title: Download and unzip
steps.text: Get the zip from Eric Zimmerman's tools page. Pick the .NET 4 build or the .NET 10 build, depending on which runtime your computer has. Unzip it with 7-Zip into a folder such as C:\Tools\MFTECmd.

steps.title: Get the file you want to parse
steps.text: Copy $MFT out of your evidence first. Work on a copy or a mounted image, never on the original. The tool can also read locked files from a live disk, but for case work use a forensic image.

steps.title: Open a command prompt in the folder
steps.text: Start Command Prompt or PowerShell and change to the folder that holds MFTECmd.exe. Run the tool with no options if you want to see its help text.

steps.title: Parse the $MFT to CSV
steps.text: Use -f for the input file and --csv for the output folder. Put the paths in quotes. The tool writes a CSV file with a name based on the time of the run. Add --csvf to choose the file name yourself.

steps.title: Look at one entry in detail
steps.text: To inspect a single record, give its entry number and sequence number to --de. This prints the full details on screen. Use it when a row in the CSV looks odd.

steps.title: Open the CSV in a viewer
steps.text: Load the CSV in Timeline Explorer, or in a spreadsheet, so you can sort and filter millions of rows. Sort by time, filter on a path or a name, and note the entry numbers you want to follow up.

steps.title: Parse the USN journal as well
steps.text: Run the same command with $J as the input to get file create, rename and delete activity. Add the $MFT with -m so the tool can fill in the parent paths. The project README documents -m for this purpose.

options.what: Writes CSV results to this folder. Use --csvf to set the file name.
Writes JSON results to this folder. Use --jsonf to set the file name.
Writes a bodyfile. --bdl sets the drive letter to use in the paths.
Shows full details for one entry number or entry-sequence number, such as 5 or 624-5.
Exports one raw FILE record from the given offset (decimal or hex).
Processes all Volume Shadow Copies on the drive given with -f.
Removes duplicate files between the drive and its shadow copies using SHA-1. The first file found is kept.
Includes all timestamps from the 0x30 attribute, not only the ones that differ from the 0x10 attribute.

cases.title: Timestomping checks
cases.why: Each record holds two sets of times. A tampered file may show different values in the two sets. The tool leaves the second set empty when they match, which helps you spot the files that differ.

cases.title: Data theft and staging
cases.why: Sort the file list by time and size to find large files or archives created in a short window before an incident.

cases.title: Deleted file evidence
cases.why: The listing includes entries for deleted files, with a flag showing whether the record is still in use. This shows that a file existed even if it is gone.

cases.title: Timeline building
cases.why: Bodyfile and CSV output can be merged with results from other tools to place file activity in order with events from other artifacts.

cases.title: Malware investigation
cases.why: File creation times and paths show when a suspicious program appeared and which other files were written near it.

cases.title: Comparing older versions of a volume
cases.why: With shadow copy support you can parse earlier states of the volume and see what changed between them.

strengths: Free, with the source code published under the MIT licence.
Handles several NTFS system files with one tool and one set of options.
Output goes straight into CSV viewers and timeline workflows.
The project reports faster loading of large $MFT files in its 2026.10 changelog.
limits: It is a command-line tool with many options, so the first runs take some practice.
It only reads NTFS metadata. It does not recover file contents, except for small resident data where the options allow it.
It works on Windows. The file must first be copied out of your evidence.
The README does not describe the exact output fields, so learn the columns by looking at a sample CSV.
Its convenience flags are produced by the tool, not stored in the raw $MFT. Check suspicious files against the full record and the case context.
The CSV for a large volume can be very big and may be slow to open in a spreadsheet.
